title: A Generation in Search of Representation: Why Spain’s Youth Embraces Radicalism
dek: How did a generation raised in democracy become drawn to political extremes?
author: Yann Grechez Elkoubi
hero_caption: Far-right supporters raise their right arms in salute as they commemorate former Spanish dictator Francisco Franco on the 39th anniversary of his death in Madrid
body:
Almost half of Gen Z men and a quarter of Gen Z women in Spain say they plan to vote for the far right in the upcoming elections. Once seen as a driving force in Spain's transition from fascism to democracy, young people in Spain are now increasingly drawn to illiberal radical politics. What exactly happened?

Most research explains populist support through major political shocks (2008 crisis, 2014 immigration, 2017 secession, 2020 pandemic) or traditional socioeconomic factors (income, education level, gender), but these approaches struggle to explain why young Spaniards across all income levels, regions, genders, and educational backgrounds are increasingly backing populist parties.

Instead, we must take a look at the larger political, cultural, social, and economic shifts that have developed specifically during Gen Z’s timeframe that are driving this exceptional support for populism. 

A major study in the Political Science world is The Populist Zeitgeist by Cas Mudde, the leading scholar of populism. In this study, Mudde proposes several generational shifts that he believes best explain why the youth are turning to populism at unprecedented levels. He proposes a framework of 5 key reasons explaining the rise of populism in the West. In reference to Spain, three key points stand out as most significant.

sections.alt: A child raises his fist during a demonstration in Madrid’s Calle Preciados, June 22, 1976. Photo: César Lucas/El País.
sections.caption: A child raises his fist during a demonstration in Madrid’s Calle Preciados, June 22, 1976 (César Lucas/El País)

sections.body:
A major trend shaping Spain’s Gen Z is a growing dissatisfaction with democracy and the institutions designed to uphold it. Political scientists often distinguish between specific support, meaning satisfaction with how democratic institutions are currently performing, and diffuse support, a deeper belief that democracy is the best political system overall.

Generally, research finds that diffuse support for democracy (the belief that democracy is the best political model) is not affected by declining specific support (discontent with the current performance of one’s government). However, young Spaniards appear to be breaking this trend, as Gen Z shows lower diffuse support for democracy than older generations.

In other words, young Spaniards are not just frustrated with their politicians or parties; they are becoming less convinced that democracy is the best political system. A loss of commitment to democratic values creates fertile ground for populist parties with centralized, charismatic leadership who promise to bring power from the elites to “the people”.

sections.alt: EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and Spain’s Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez during an EU summit in Madrid. (AP Photo/Bernat Armangue)
sections.caption: EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and Spain’s Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez during an EU summit in Madrid. (AP Photo/Bernat Armangue)

sections.body:
Another important force shaping Spain’s Gen Z is the growing influence of the European Union and the broader shift toward technocratic politics. In simple terms, more political decisions are now made beyond the national level, often by institutions that feel distant, technical, and difficult for ordinary citizens to influence or feel a part of.

There is a growing sensation amongst Gen Z that politics is no longer fully decided through national elections or public debate, but through complex institutions that they do not feel represented by or believe they can influence.

As more authority moves to organizations such as the European Commission or the European Central Bank, key policy choices can feel removed from everyday democratic contestation. For young voters, this deepens the impression that liberal politics are unresponsive, inaccessible, and incapable of representing their concerns.

In Spain, this sense of distance from the EU appears especially relevant among younger generations, as Eurobarometer data also shows that only around a third of Spaniards aged 15 to 24 believe their voice counts in the EU. This perceived loss of political agency makes space for populist parties, which claim to return decision-making to, once again, “the actual people”.

sections.alt: A child playing on a phone in Barcelona in 2024. (Emilio Morenatti/Associated Press)
sections.caption: A child playing on a phone in Barcelona in 2024. (Emilio Morenatti/Associated Press)

sections.body:
Lastly, informational media has been democratized. Today anyone can produce, consume, and share any type of political information they desire. Although this has made political information more accessible, it has also created a sensational and unfiltered informational climate that naturally favors the growth of scandalous and divisive rhetoric.

Media algorithms that favor engagement over accuracy often reward content that is emotional and extreme, content that receives more likes, comments, and shares, ultimately making “us versus them” populist narratives more prominent.

Young Spaniards encounter politics through personalized feeds, viral clips, and emotionally charged content that is often absorbed quickly and without much discussion. This gives parties that know how to dominate online spaces a major advantage in capturing young voters.

Research suggests that Vox and Podemos are among the most visible and engaging parties in the online political environment young Spaniards are exposed to. When most Gen Z Spaniards now rely on social media as their main source of political news, and populist parties seem to be the ones making the most noise on them, it becomes easier to understand why they have such great success among young voters.

sections.alt: Supporters of Spain’s far-right Vox party attend an election campaign rally in Madrid (Bernat Armangue/AP)
sections.caption: Supporters of Spain’s far-right Vox party attend an election campaign rally in Madrid (Bernat Armangue/AP)

sections.body:
By isolating the structural developments in Gen Z’s formative context that are closely linked to populist support, we can prescribe policy that more meaningfully combats the rise in radicalization and affective polarization.

The transformation of the media landscape, the democratic disillusionment, and the perceived loss of political agency young people are experiencing are three areas that are rapidly mobilizing support for radical populism, and that are definitely worth looking into for policymakers.

These concerns call for policies such as online safeguards and educational programs aimed at enhancing digital literacy among younger cohorts, teaching them how to navigate such a polarized and unfiltered informational climate. They also call for changes in democratic representation, opening the door to more direct and participatory forms of democracy, or educational curricula that emphasize the importance of democracy and what it looks like when it is gone, which is something the Spanish youth seems to be forgetting.
